change.title: pr-33832-flat
change.description: Add AuthzClientCryptoProvider for authorization client cryptographic operations
change.author: Cristian Sotomayor

findings.title: Ambiguous provider sets no longer fail; a tie is resolved silently
findings.body: The old code threw `IllegalStateException` when more than one `CryptoProvider` was on the classpath. Now the list is sorted by `order()` and the first entry wins, and the ignored providers are only logged at DEBUG (lines 64-70). `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider` and `WildFlyElytronProvider` all return 200. If a FIPS or Elytron deployment also has `crypto-default` on the classpath by mistake, two providers tie at 200. The `sorted` call is stable, so the winner is whichever `ServiceLoader` returns first, which depends on classpath order. The server then starts with a possibly non-FIPS provider and logs nothing above DEBUG. The new `order()` only needs to let the authz-client provider (100) lose to a real one. Keep the fail-fast when the top two providers share the same `order()`, and throw the existing 'Multiple crypto providers' error in that case.

findings.title: debugf called with a pre-built string as the format
findings.body: `logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes the concatenated class names as a format string. The message also ends with a trailing ", ". Use `logger.debugf("Ignored crypto providers: %s", ...)` with a joined list, for example `Collectors.joining(", ")`.

findings.title: Dead code: two encodings are built and discarded
findings.body: Lines 114-115 create `ASN1Encoder` instances and write r and s, then throw the results away. The same encodings are rebuilt in the `return` statement at lines 117-121. Delete the two lines.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default KeyStore provider, which becomes BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER
findings.body: `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` is a static final set from `getBouncyCastleProvider().getName()` (`common/.../BouncyIntegration.java:31-39`). With this provider it becomes the name of whatever JDK provider backs the default keystore type, probably "SUN". Any shared code that calls `X.getInstance(alg, BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER)` on this path would ask that provider for an algorithm it may not have, for example RSA `KeyFactory` or `Signature`. The `getKeyFactory`, `getSignature` and similar methods here throw `UnsupportedOperationException`, so that is the only path that can reach it today. The method name and the `KeyStore` lookup are misleading. Either return `null`, which `BouncyIntegration` handles by using `Security.getProviders()[0]`, or add a comment saying why the keystore provider is used.

findings.title: First-wins init can lock in the stripped-down provider when jars sit in different classloaders
findings.body: `CryptoIntegration.init` only detects a provider while `cryptoProvider == null`. It searches with `AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()`. If the authz-client jar is in a parent or shared classloader and the application's real provider (BC or FIPS) is only visible to a child classloader, this call runs first. It finds only `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` and sets it. A later `CryptoIntegration.init(appLoader)` then does nothing. Every other operation (`getKeyFactory`, `getSignature`, `getCertificateUtils` and so on) throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. Was this layout considered? If it matters, `init` could be skipped when a provider is already set, or the context classloader could be tried first.

findings.title: Round-trip test is self-consistent only and uses a P-256 key for ES384/ES512
findings.body: The test checks `der -> RS -> der -> RS` and compares the two RS arrays. A consistent bug in the encoder and decoder would still pass, and the DER is never checked against the JDK. Verify `asn1Des` with `Signature.initVerify(publicKey).verify(asn1Des)` (the DER re-encoding is what `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` feeds to the verifier), and compare it to the original `sign`. The key is a default `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` key (P-256, line 42) for all three algorithms. ES384 and ES512 therefore only exercise 32-byte r and s zero-padded to 48 or 66 bytes. They never use a full-width value with the high bit set, which is the case that needs the leading 0x00 byte. Generate the key with the matching curve (`secp384r1`, `secp521r1`) and loop several times so short-r and high-bit cases occur. The tests also do not cover `ServiceLoader` selection or `order()` (authz provider loses to a real one), which is the other behaviour this change adds.

contracts.equivalent_path: Other entry points call CryptoIntegration.init at startup, for example the server and adapters.
contracts.before_after: Before: the authz client never initialised CryptoIntegration, so any core code calling getProvider() threw IllegalStateException. After: the first create() detects a provider through ServiceLoader. create() and create(InputStream) both delegate to create(Configuration) (AuthzClient.java:63,82), so every factory is covered.
contracts.visible_effect: ECDSA signature conversion in core (ECDSAAlgorithm) works in a bare authz-client app. Other provider operations throw UnsupportedOperationException instead of IllegalStateException.
contracts.failure_mode: If no provider is found, init throws IllegalStateException from create(). If the authz-client jar is in a shared classloader, its provider may win and block the real one (see finding).

contracts.action: Provider selection changed from fail-on-multiple to sort-by-order and pick the first
contracts.equivalent_path: The previous detectProvider threw when more than one provider was found.
contracts.before_after: Before: a misconfigured classpath failed fast. After: the highest order() wins, and the ignored providers are logged at DEBUG only. Default, FIPS and Elytron all return 200 and the authz client returns 100. A tie at 200 is resolved by ServiceLoader order.
contracts.visible_effect: The authz-client-tests jar on the Keycloak testsuite classpath no longer breaks startup. A mixed FIPS and default classpath is now accepted silently.
contracts.failure_mode: Silent selection of the wrong provider on a tie (see finding).

contracts.action: AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider converts between concatenated R||S and ASN.1 DER using the new ASN1Encoder and ASN1Decoder
contracts.equivalent_path: BCECDSACryptoProvider, in the default, FIPS and Elytron providers, is reached through ECDSAAlgorithm in core. ECDSASignatureVerifierContext calls concatenatedRSToASN1DER, and ECDSASignatureSignerContext calls asn1derToConcatenatedRS.
contracts.before_after: The call chain is the same, and the new code gives the same result for well-formed input. The encoder prefixes a zero byte so r and s are non-negative. The decoder re-pads or truncates to len bytes.
contracts.visible_effect: ES256, ES384 and ES512 signature conversion works without BouncyCastle. Signing and verifying still need getSignature and getKeyFactory, which throw UnsupportedOperationException here.
contracts.failure_mode: A signature shorter than signLength gives ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. The verifier wraps it in VerificationException (ECDSASignatureVerifierContext.java:32-33), so there is no crash. Malformed DER gives IOException.

summary:
I read all 12 files and found no blockers. The main concern is `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider`: it no longer fails when several providers are on the classpath. Default, FIPS and Elytron all return order 200, so a mixed classpath now picks one silently, with only a DEBUG log. I suggest keeping the fail-fast when the top two orders tie.

Smaller points:
- **Dead code:** `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` builds and discards two ASN.1 encodings at lines 114-115.
- **Misleading provider:** `getBouncyCastleProvider` returns the default `KeyStore` provider, which then becomes `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER`.
- **Classloader risk (question, low confidence):** `AuthzClient.create` does a first-wins `init`, so with a shared classloader the stripped-down provider could be locked in.
- **Test:** `ECDSAAlgorithmTest` is a round trip that only uses a P-256 key, even for ES384 and ES512, and never checks the DER against the JDK.

I only read the code and did not build or run it.
